generation.hypothesis: A FeCoNiTi-based high-entropy alloy with a tuned elemental composition (by adjusting the Fe, Co, Ni, and Ti ratios) will exhibit an enhanced magnetocaloric effect near room temperature compared to conventional Gd-based alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A standard FeCoNiTi high-entropy alloy with multiphase (fcc and possibly minor additional phase) magnetic structure.
generation.intervention: Adjust the elemental ratios in the FeCoNiTi alloy to fine-tune its magnetic transition temperatures closer to room temperature and to amplify the magnetic entropy change.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted near room temperature under moderate magnetic field strengths typical for magnetic refrigeration conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Tunable multiphase microstructure that enables multiple ferromagnetic transitions, likely through adjusting phase fractions and atomic-scale disorder.
generation.mechanism: Compositional adjustment modifies the magnetic exchange interactions and shifts the ferromagnetic transition temperatures, thereby enhancing the magnetic entropy change through the emergence of multiple, closely spaced magnetic transitions.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in the magnetic entropy change at room temperature, leading to improved magnetocaloric performance over conventional Gd-based materials.
generation.baseline: Performance levels of current Gd-based alloys, which exhibit only moderate magnetocaloric effects at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only within a limited compositional window; deviation from the optimized ratios may lead to unwanted phase segregation or deteriorated magnetic performance.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement in the magnetocaloric effect is uncertain due to the complex interplay of magnetic interactions and phase stability in multi-component systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of FeCoNiTi-based high-entropy alloy samples with systematically varied elemental ratios. Characterize their phase structures by X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy, and measure magnetization as a function of temperature and applied magnetic field.
measurements: Magnetic entropy change (ΔS_mag) near room temperature
Phase composition and microstructure via XRD/SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if no sample shows a significant enhancement in magnetic entropy change near room temperature compared to a baseline Gd-based alloy, or if tuning the composition results in degraded magnetic properties or adverse phase stability.

cited_evidence.text:
A high-entropy alloy (HEA) is delineated as an alloy comprising multiple principal elements with an almost equiatomic composition. [1] , [2] The thermodynamic evaluation of alloy entropy is executed through configurational entropy, denoted as Δ S mix = − R ∑ i = 1 n c i ln c i , where n represents the number of elements, c i denotes the atomic fraction, and R is the gas constant. The established threshold value of Δ S mix , defining HEA, is presently set at 1.0 R , typically achieved by incorporating four principal elements. [3] HEAs exhibit significant promise for practical applications due to their exceptional attributes, encompassing high strength and ductility, corrosion resistance, energy storage capabilities, magnetic refrigeration, soft ferromagnetism, thermoelectricity, and superconductivity. [4] − [13]

The expansive compositional domain of HEAs affords us more freedom in designing single-phase alloys with novel properties. [14] , [15] Furthermore, the vast number of elemental combinations gives rise to multiphase HEAs, contributing to their multifaceted functionalities. decision.trend: Early work in high-entropy alloys has largely focused on tuning and optimizing mechanical properties via processing routes (e.g., HPHT treatments, thermo‐mechanical processing, additive manufacturing) while establishing compositional guidelines for high strength, ductility, and stability. More recently, researchers began to explore intrinsic properties beyond mechanics. The last paper (PMC11375712) specifically examined the magnetic behavior of an FeCoNiTi high-entropy alloy, revealing multiple ferromagnetic transitions and a high coercive field in its fcc phase. This study hints at the possibility of harnessing the complex magnetic order in these alloys to move beyond conventional Gd-based materials, though it fell short of directly establishing superior magnetocaloric performance.
decision.unsolved: While conventional Gd‐based alloys offer acceptable magnetocaloric effects, they suffer from cost, availability, and moderate performance near room temperature. The key unsolved issue remains the design of a material that not only exhibits enhanced magnetic entropy change but also operates efficiently under practical conditions. Specifically, tailoring multi‐transition behavior to coincide with room temperature and optimizing magneto-thermodynamic parameters for cooling applications have not yet been achieved.
decision.lever: Tuning the elemental composition of high-entropy alloys (e.g., by adjusting the Fe, Co, Ni, and Ti ratios) to shift magnetic transition temperatures closer to room temperature and boost the magnetic entropy change.
decision.why: Building on the trend from mechanical-property optimization toward exploiting multifunctional properties in HEAs, the magnetic analysis in FeCoNiTi suggests these alloys’ magnetic transitions are tunable by compositional adjustment. This approach directly addresses the magnetocaloric limitation by aiming for enhanced magnetocaloric effects and practical operating conditions, following cues from the transition from conventional Gd-based systems.
